title: The Charybdis of the Faubourg Saint Antoine and the Scylla
summary: Opening the last volume, Hugo steps forward sixteen years to describe the two colossal barricades of June 1848, the furious Saint-Antoine heap and the silent, geometric wall of the Faubourg du Temple, and the two men who built them, so that the reader can measure the small barricade of 1832 against them.
details: Hugo begins Volume V with a digression he insists is not one. The two most memorable barricades he knows belong not to 1832 but to June 1848, when, in the greatest street war in history, the rabble rose against the people and the republic itself had to be fought in the name of the republic. He pronounces the words beggars, canaille and populace with pain and respect: the populace saved Rome, the rabble followed Christ, and when the suffering crowd attacks the very principles that are its life, the honest man must resist it with a sad conscience.

The Saint-Antoine barricade was three storeys high and seven hundred feet wide, built of demolished houses, carts, an omnibus hoisted to the summit, doors, gratings and rags, with nineteen more barricades ranged behind it. It converted everything into a weapon, firing coat-buttons and bits of crockery, crowned with a red flag and a tumult of shouts and songs: a heap of filth and a Sinai. A quarter of a league away the barricade of the Faubourg du Temple was its opposite, a straight wall of paving-stones laid out by rule and line, pierced with invisible loopholes, in a street where nothing moved and every passer-by fell to an unseen marksman. Eighty men held it for three days against ten thousand; when it was taken through the houses and over the roofs, all died but their leader.

The first was a dragon, the second a sphinx. Hugo names their builders, Cournet, a huge, stormy former naval officer with something of Danton in him, and Barthélemy, a thin, pale street urchin who had killed a policeman at seventeen and come out of the galleys to build this wall. He adds their epilogue: years later in London Barthélemy killed Cournet in a duel and was afterwards hanged, a man of real intelligence whom destitution carried from the French galleys to the English gallows.

title: What Is to Be Done in the Abyss if One Does Not Converse
summary: Back in the Rue de la Chanvrerie, the insurgents spend the night raising and repairing the barricade, laying out their dead and nursing the wounded; by dawn thirty-seven remain, hungry, with Mabeuf's body and the bound Javert in the taproom, and the talk turns to philosophy as the day breaks.
details: Compared with the giants of 1848, the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie was an embryo, but it was formidable for its day. Under Enjolras, since Marius no longer attended to anything, the insurgents used the night well: the wall was raised two feet and bristled with iron bars, the paving-stone staircase rebuilt, the taproom cleared, the kitchen turned into an ambulance, bullets cast and cartridges made. The dead were heaped in the Mondétour lane; among them were four suburban National Guardsmen, and Enjolras had their uniforms set aside. Feuilly spent the two hours of ordered rest carving "Long live the peoples!" on the wall with a nail. The three women of the house had slipped away to a neighbouring house.

Five badly wounded men, two of them municipal guards, lay on mattresses in the kitchen, the guards attended to first. In the taproom only Mabeuf under his black cloth and Javert bound to his post remained; Enjolras called it the hall of the dead, and the upright prisoner and the prone corpse made a kind of cross in the candlelight. Enjolras fastened the old man's bullet-riddled coat to the broken omnibus pole as the flag. There was nothing to eat; Enjolras forbade wine and rationed the brandy, and fifteen sealed bottles found in the cellar, Father Hucheloup's old stock, he placed under Mabeuf's table with a veto on them, Bossuet remarking how lucky it was that Grantaire was asleep. At two in the morning they counted thirty-seven men.

Dawn came pale over the roofs, birds crying in the sky and the breeze stirring the hair of the dead man in the third-storey window. Courfeyrac was glad the trembling torch was out. Joly drew a theory of creation from a cat on a gutter; Combeferre spoke of the dead, of Jean Prouvaire, Bahorel, Mabeuf and even Le Cabuc, and of how even a liberating killing leaves more remorse than joy, then drifted through translators of the Georgics to Caesar and Brutus, judging Caesar's fall just but finding the spitting on Christ a greater outrage than Caesar's twenty-three wounds. Bossuet, on his heap of stones with a rifle, cried out for Homer in Greek.

title: Light and Shadow
summary: Enjolras returns from a reconnaissance to tell the hopeful insurgents the truth: a third of the army is coming, Paris is not rising, and they are abandoned; an unknown man answers that they should stay and offer the protest of corpses, and all acclaim him.
details: The insurgents were full of hope. Having beaten off the night attack, they almost disdained the one to come, and they mapped out the day: a regiment would go over to them at six, all Paris would rise at noon, revolution by sunset. The alarm bell of Saint-Merry, ringing without pause, proved that the other great barricade still held. Their hopes hummed from group to group like a hive.

Enjolras, who had slipped out along the Mondétour lane to look, came back and listened for a moment with folded arms. Then he told them plainly: the whole army of Paris was to strike, a third of it was bearing down on this barricade, with the National Guard besides; he had seen the shakos of the fifth of the line and the standards of the sixth legion; they would be attacked within the hour; the populace that had seethed yesterday was not stirring today. Nothing to expect, nothing to hope for. "You are abandoned." A silence fell in which death might have been heard passing.

It was brief. A voice from the darkest part of the groups answered: so be it, raise the barricade to twenty feet and all stay in it; let them offer the protest of corpses and show that if the people abandon the republicans, the republicans do not abandon the people. The words freed every man from his private fears and were hailed with enthusiasm. No one ever knew who spoke; he was some unknown man in a blouse, the anonymous hero who in a crisis says the decisive word and vanishes. At almost the same hour, Hugo notes, the insurgents of Saint-Merry were shouting the same resolve to die to the last man.

title: Minus Five, Plus One
summary: Enjolras, Combeferre and Marius persuade the insurgents that fathers and breadwinners must leave in the four captured uniforms; five are chosen but there are only four uniforms, until a fifth falls on the pile: Jean Valjean, in his National Guard dress, has entered the barricade, and Marius recognises him as M. Fauchelevent.
details: The cry went up: long live death, let us all stay. Enjolras objected that thirty men were enough to hold the position and that the republic was not rich enough in men to waste forty. The murmurs grew; someone pointed out that the barricade was hemmed in anyway, and that a man in a blouse smelling of powder would be shot the moment he reached the Halles. Enjolras and Combeferre fetched the four National Guard uniforms with their belts and shakos and threw them on the ground: dressed in these, four men could mingle with the troops and escape. No one moved.

Combeferre then made a long appeal. It was a question of women and children: of mothers watching at candlelit windows, of daughters who, left without bread, would be driven to the street and the police, of small children left to starve, like the one he had seen as a house-surgeon at the Necker Hospital, dead with ashes in his teeth and mud in his stomach. To die was fine; to make others die was murder. Heads dropped. Hugo notes the contradiction: Combeferre, who was not an orphan, remembered other men's mothers and forgot his own.

Marius, fevered and fasting, sunk in the stupor of a man who has accepted death, was roused by this one thing: he could save someone else while destroying himself. He added his entreaty to Enjolras's order, and the men began denouncing one another as fathers and breadwinners. Enjolras had them vote; five were chosen unanimously. But there were only four uniforms, and the five began a generous quarrel over who should stay. They asked Marius to choose, and he counted them with horror, each crying "Me!"

At that moment a fifth uniform fell on the pile. Marius looked up and recognised M. Fauchelevent. Jean Valjean had come in by the Mondétour lane, admitted by the sentinel as a lone National Guardsman, and had silently taken off his coat. Bossuet asked who he was; Combeferre said, a man who saves others; Marius said, "I know him." Enjolras welcomed him as a citizen and told him they were about to die. Without replying, Valjean helped the fifth man into his uniform.

title: The Horizon Which One Beholds from the Summit of a Barricade
summary: Standing on the paving-stone staircase, Enjolras delivers a prophetic speech on the future: a world of light, equal schooling, the union of peoples, liberty, equality and fraternity defined, the happy twentieth century, and this barricade as the meeting of ideas and woes where those who die enter a tomb flooded with dawn.
details: Hugo pauses on Enjolras's state of mind. He carried the whole revolution in him, with too much of Saint-Just and not enough of Anacharsis Cloots, but Combeferre's influence had widened him towards the idea of a human republic; in means, though, he remained violent, of the school of '93. Leaning on his gun on the stairway of stones, he seemed to quiver with prophecy, then threw back his blond head and spoke.

He pictured the future: cities flooded with light, nations as sisters, the workshop and the school as brothers, work and right and peace for all, no more bloodshed or war. Man had conquered the hydra in the locomotive and was about to conquer the griffin in the balloon; science would become government, Europe and then the globe would have their amphictyons, a parliament of intelligence. He saluted Feuilly, the orphan artisan who had adopted humanity for his mother. Whatever happened, defeat or victory, they were making a revolution, the revolution of the True. He defined the sovereignty of each man over himself as liberty, the equal concession each makes to all as equality, the protection of all over each as fraternity, and named equality's organ: free and compulsory instruction, the right to the alphabet. The nineteenth century is great, he said, but the twentieth will be happy, with no more conquest, famine, prostitution or scaffold.

Then he turned to where they stood. The hour was gloomy, but revolutions are a toll paid for the future. This barricade was not made of stones and joists but of two heaps, a heap of ideas and a heap of woes; here misery met the ideal, the day embraced the night and promised it rebirth. Whoever died here died in the radiance of the future; they were entering a tomb all flooded with dawn. He paused rather than stopped, his lips still moving, and there was no applause, only a long whispering like the rustling of leaves.

title: Marius Haggard, Javert Laconic
summary: Marius, already feeling himself dead, does not ask why M. Fauchelevent has come; the five chosen men leave in uniform; Enjolras gives Javert water and has him moved from the post to the table, bound with a martingale, and as he is tied Javert looks up and recognises Jean Valjean, remarking only that it is perfectly simple.
details: Marius saw everything now as a man already beyond the wall of the tomb. He did not ask himself how or why M. Fauchelevent had come; in his despair it seemed natural that the whole world should come there to die, though he thought of Cosette with a pang. Fauchelevent did not speak to him or look at him, even when Marius vouched for him, and this suited Marius, who had always found it impossible to address that enigmatic and imposing man.

The five men chosen to live left by the Mondétour lane looking exactly like National Guardsmen; one wept, and they embraced those who stayed. Then Enjolras remembered the man condemned to death. Javert, still bound to the post, asked only when they meant to kill him; Enjolras answered that they needed every cartridge for the present, and when Javert asked for a drink, held a glass of water to his lips himself. Javert complained that they might at least lay him on a table like "that other man," nodding towards Mabeuf's body.

Four insurgents untied him while a fifth held a bayonet to his chest. They left his arms bound behind him, hobbled his feet with a cord that allowed steps of fifteen inches, walked him to the long table where cartridges had been made and laid him down bound about the middle, adding a rope from his neck forking over the stomach to his hands, the bond prisons call a martingale. As they worked, a man standing in the doorway watched with singular attention; his shadow made Javert turn his head. He looked up and recognised Jean Valjean. He did not start; he lowered his eyelids proudly and said only, "It is perfectly simple."

title: The Situation Becomes Aggravated
summary: At daylight the insurgents wall up the Mondétour lane, leaving themselves a fortress with no exit, and take their posts; a cannon is rolled into the street, its first ball buries itself harmlessly in the rubbish, and at that instant Gavroche leaps back into the barricade.
details: The dawn brought no awakening: not a window opened, the Rue Saint-Denis lay silent as an avenue of sphinxes, and all the sentinels came in. On the advice of the man who had scouted towards the Halles, Enjolras, fearing a surprise from the rear, had the Mondétour lane barricaded too, tearing up more pavement. The redoubt now had three fronts and no exit; "a fortress but a rat hole too," laughed Courfeyrac. Some thirty spare paving-stones were piled by the wine-shop door, brandy was doled out, and each man picked his place as at the theatre; peril, Hugo observes, produces order. When Enjolras took his double-barrelled rifle to his embrasure, the only sound was the cocking of guns.

From the Saint-Leu quarter came a clank of chains and iron: a cannon appeared, pushed by its gunners, the lint-stock already smoking. Enjolras ordered fire and the whole barricade let off a volley, but when the smoke cleared not a gunner had been hit, and the captain of the piece was levelling his gun with the gravity of an astronomer. Bossuet cried bravo for the cannoneers, and the barricade applauded. Courfeyrac welcomed the brutal part; Combeferre discoursed on the brass eight-pounder's tendency to burst, on hooping and rifling, and concluded that a cannonball travels six hundred leagues an hour while light travels seventy thousand a second, the superiority of Christ over Napoleon.

The shot came. At the same instant a joyous voice shouted "Present!" and Gavroche flung himself over the auxiliary barricade from the Rue du Cygne as the ball struck. He made a greater sensation than the cannonball, which buried itself in the heap, breaking an omnibus wheel and finishing the old Anceau cart. The barricade burst out laughing and Bossuet shouted to the gunners to go on.

title: The Artillerymen Compel People to Take Them Seriously
summary: Gavroche lies to Marius that he delivered the letter, says he does not know M. Fauchelevent, and reports that the barricade is surrounded; the cannon switches to grapeshot, killing two and wounding three, and Enjolras, weeping, shoots the young artillery sergeant to gain a few minutes.
details: Marius drew Gavroche aside and asked sternly who had told him to come back and whether he had delivered the letter. Gavroche, uneasy at having handed it to a bareheaded stranger whose face he could not see, lied: he had given it to the porter, and the lady would have it when she woke. Marius had meant the letter to bid Cosette farewell and to save Gavroche; he had to be content with half. It occurred to him that the letter and M. Fauchelevent's arrival might be connected, but Gavroche, who had only ever seen the man at night, said he did not know him, and Marius's uneasy conjectures dissolved: perhaps Fauchelevent was simply a republican.

Gavroche got his gun back from Courfeyrac and told his comrades the barricade was blocked: a line battalion in the Rue de la Petite Truanderie watched the Rue du Cygne, the municipal guard held the Rue des Prêcheurs, the bulk of the army was in front. He authorised them to hit the enemy a tremendous whack. Meanwhile infantry occupied the end of the street behind the gun and built a low wall of paving-stones, and Enjolras heard grapeshot being drawn from the caissons and saw the muzzle shifted slightly to the left. He shouted to everyone to kneel along the wall, but the men who had left their posts to crowd round Gavroche were too slow: the charge struck the cut in the redoubt, rebounded off the wall and left two dead and three wounded. If this went on the barricade was untenable.

Enjolras resolved to prevent the second discharge and took aim at the captain of the gun, a very young, blond sergeant with a gentle, intelligent face. Combeferre, beside him, begged him to look at the man: he had a family, he was probably in love, he might be your brother. "He is," said Enjolras; "he is mine too," said Combeferre, "let us not kill him." "Let me alone. It must be done." A tear ran down Enjolras's marble cheek as he fired. The sergeant turned twice with arms outstretched and fell dead across his gun, shot through the breast. Several minutes were gained while he was replaced.

title: Employment of the Old Talents of a Poacher and That Infallible Marksmanship Which Influenced the Condemnation of 1796
summary: To deaden the grapeshot a mattress is needed; Jean Valjean borrows Enjolras's rifle, shoots through the two ropes holding an old woman's mattress across a distant attic window, walks out through the fusillade to fetch it, and plugs the breach, and Enjolras thanks him in the name of the Republic.
details: The gun would fire again within minutes and the barricade could not survive a quarter of an hour of grapeshot. Enjolras ordered a mattress placed in the cut; Combeferre answered that the wounded were lying on all of them. Jean Valjean, who had sat apart on a stone post by the tavern with his gun across his knees, deaf to remarks about a gun that was doing nothing, rose at the order.

He remembered the old woman who, foreseeing bullets, had hung her mattress across her attic window on the roof of a six-storey house a little beyond the barricade; it hung from two ropes that looked like threads against the sky. He asked for a double-barrelled rifle, and Enjolras handed him his own. Valjean fired and cut one rope; he fired again and the second rope whipped the panes, and the mattress slid between its poles and fell into the street. The barricade applauded, but it had landed between besiegers and besieged, and the soldiers, enraged by the sergeant's death and lying behind their stone wall, were pouring musketry into the street while the gun was re-crewed.

Valjean stepped out of the cut, walked through the storm of bullets, hoisted the mattress on his back, returned and fixed it in the breach with his own hands, hidden from the gunners. The next discharge of grapeshot roared against it and did not rebound. The barricade was saved. "Citizen," said Enjolras, "the Republic thanks you." Bossuet laughed at the immorality of a mattress with so much power: glory to the thing that yields, which annuls a cannon.

title: Dawn
summary: At the same hour Cosette wakes in the Rue de l'Homme Armé knowing nothing of the fighting, sure that Marius has had her letter and will come today; she can see nothing of the street, mistakes the distant cannon for carriage gates, and watches a martins' nest below her window.
details: Cosette woke with the sun in her eyes in her narrow room over the back courtyard. She had not been out the evening before and had gone to bed before Toussaint mentioned "a row"; she knew nothing of what was happening in Paris. She had dreamed of Marius and woke smiling, filled, like Jean Valjean a few hours earlier, with a reaction of the soul that refuses unhappiness. It was three days since she had seen Marius, but he must have her letter, he knew where she was, and he was clever enough to find a way to her, surely today, perhaps this very morning. She was vexed that she could not remember what he had told her about an absence that was to last only a day.

Hugo declines to describe a young girl's rising: one may show a nuptial chamber but not a virginal one, and here contemplation would be profanation. Cosette dressed hastily and opened her window hoping for a scrap of street to watch for Marius, but the court was walled in and looked only onto gardens, which for the first time in her life she found ugly. She decided to watch the sky instead, as if he might come from there. Suddenly she burst into tears, with a confused sense of something horrible in the air, then calm and hope returned.

The house still slept; the porter's lodge was shut, Toussaint had not risen, and Cosette supposed her father asleep too. She told herself he had been unkind, but she counted on Marius. Now and then she heard sharp shocks in the distance and thought it odd that people were opening and shutting their carriage gates so early: it was the cannon battering the barricade. A few feet below her window a martin's nest sat in the black cornice, the mother spread over her brood, the father flying to and fro with food; Cosette, her hair in the sun, leaned over and gazed at that small family with the profound trouble a nest produces in a virgin.

title: The Shot Which Misses Nothing and Kills No One
summary: The besiegers keep up a fire meant to exhaust the barricade's ammunition, and Enjolras does not reply; when a fireman and then an officer appear on a roof to spy on the redoubt, Jean Valjean knocks the helmet off each with a bullet and the watchers withdraw, and he will not say why he did not kill them.
details: Musketry and grapeshot alternated without doing much harm except to the top of the Corinthe façade, whose first-floor window and attic were slowly losing their shape, forcing the men posted there to withdraw. Hugo explains the tactic: fire for a long time to make the insurgents waste their powder, then assault when their fire slackens. Enjolras did not fall into the trap, and the barricade stayed silent. Gavroche puffed out his cheek in disdain at each volley and asked the soldiers to rip up more cloth, since they wanted lint; Courfeyrac told the cannon it was growing diffuse.

The silence seemed to worry the besiegers, who needed to see what was going on behind that wall. A fireman's helmet glittered on a neighbouring roof, its wearer standing against a chimney with his glance falling straight into the barricade. "There's an embarrassing watcher," said Enjolras. Jean Valjean, who had returned Enjolras's rifle but had his own gun, took aim without a word, and a second later the helmet, smashed by a bullet, rattled into the street; the terrified man vanished. An officer took his place, and Valjean, reloading, sent his casque after the fireman's. No one appeared on that roof again.
Bossuet asked Valjean why he had not killed the man. Jean Valjean made no reply.

title: Disorder a Partisan of Order
summary: Hugo describes the zealous, undisciplined suburban National Guard of 1832, whose improvised firing squads had killed Jean Prouvaire, and tells how Captain Fannicot, impatient with his generals, hurled his company at the barricade on his own initiative, lost fifteen men and then died under his own side's grapeshot, to Enjolras's irritation.
details: Bossuet muttered to Combeferre that the man had not answered his question; Combeferre replied that he was a man who does good by gunshots. Hugo then turns to the suburban National Guard, valiant against insurrection in June 1832: dram-shop keepers who became lions over a closed dance-hall, bankers who sang the Marseillaise as their piles of crowns shrank, shopkeepers defending the shop with Spartan enthusiasm. It was serious underneath, social elements in strife, but it mixed order with a lack of discipline. Colonels beat capricious drum calls, captains went into action by inspiration, and platoons set themselves up as councils of war to judge and shoot a captured insurgent in five minutes; such an improvisation had killed Jean Prouvaire, and a young poet was nearly killed for carrying the memoirs of the Duc de Saint-Simon.

On the 6th of June Captain Fannicot, a bold, impatient bourgeois and fanatical governmentalist, could not resist firing early. Exasperated by the red flag and by Mabeuf's old coat, which he took for a black flag, he blamed the generals who were letting the insurrection fry in its own fat and launched his company of "raging fellows" at the barricade alone. Two-thirds of the way up the street a general discharge met them; four of the boldest were mown down at the foot of the redoubt, the company wavered and fell back leaving fifteen corpses, a second volley struck it before it reached shelter, and then the cannon, which had received no order to stop, caught it between two fires. Fannicot himself died of that grapeshot, killed by order.

Enjolras was angry: the fools were getting their own men killed and using up the barricade's ammunition for nothing. He spoke, Hugo says, like the true general of insurrection he was, for insurrection has a fixed number of shots and men while repression has the army and the arsenal of Vincennes; the struggle is one against a hundred and always ends in the crushing of the barricade, unless revolution itself rises and the army, that lion, finds France, that prophet, standing before it.

title: Passing Gleams
summary: A brief hope passes over the barricade as Enjolras hears Paris stirring: for an hour or two on the morning of 6 June the insurrection flares up elsewhere, but the troops stamp it out, and the leaden indifference of the city settles back over the abandoned men, who are told they will die hungry.
details: Among the feelings that defend a barricade there are intermittences of hope, and one crossed the Rue de la Chanvrerie when it was least expected. Enjolras, still on watch, cried out that Paris seemed to be waking. It was true that on the morning of the 6th the insurrection broke out again for an hour or two. The obstinate bell of Saint-Merry revived some fancies; barricades were begun in the Rue du Poirier and the Rue des Gravilliers; at the Porte Saint-Martin a young man knelt on the open boulevard, shot the commander of a cavalry squadron and was put to the sword; a woman fired from behind a blind in the Rue Saint-Denis; a boy of fourteen was arrested with his pockets full of cartridges; cuirassiers were fired on in the Rue Bertin-Poirée, and in the Rue Planche-Mibray crockery rained from the roofs, which made Marshal Soult think of Suchet's saying at Saragossa about old women and their chamber-pots.

These symptoms disturbed the military chiefs, who hurried to put out the sparks before dealing with the barricades of Maubuée, the Chanvrerie and Saint-Merry, so as to finish them at one blow. Columns swept the streets, broke in the doors of houses that had fired, and cavalry dispersed the groups on the boulevards. This was the commotion Enjolras had caught between cannonades; he had also seen wounded men carried past the end of the street and told Courfeyrac that those wounded did not come from them.

The hope did not last half an hour: a flash of lightning without thunder. The general movement miscarried, and the war minister and the generals could now concentrate on the three or four barricades still standing. The sun climbed. An insurgent asked Enjolras whether they were really going to die like this without anything to eat; Enjolras, elbows on his embrasure, nodded without taking his eyes from the end of the street.

title: Wherein Will Appear the Name of Enjolras’ Mistress
summary: Courfeyrac and Bossuet replace food with jokes and Bossuet marvels that Enjolras is brave without a woman, while Enjolras murmurs "Patria"; a second cannon arrives, the two guns batter the crest and the windows to prepare an assault, and the barricade's answering volleys cut down most of the gunners at the cost of nearly all its cartridges, which Gavroche overhears.
details: Courfeyrac, seated on a paving-stone beside Enjolras, went on insulting the cannon each time its grapeshot passed overhead: that was not thunder, only a cough. He and Bossuet poured out gaiety in place of wine. Bossuet admired Enjolras's impassive daring and theorised that all heroism comes from women, a man without a woman being a pistol without a trigger; Enjolras had no mistress and yet managed to be as cold as ice and as bold as fire. Enjolras seemed not to listen, but anyone near him would have heard him murmur, "Patria."

Courfeyrac announced news in the tone of an usher: "My name is Eight-Pounder." A second gun had arrived and was placed in line with the first; this outlined the catastrophe. Soon both pieces were firing point-blank, supported by the platoon fire of the line and the suburbs, while two more cannon in the Rue Saint-Denis and the Rue Aubry-le-Boucher riddled the Saint-Merry barricade and the four guns barked at each other across Paris. One gun fired grapeshot, the other balls aimed high to crumble the crest onto the insurgents, the object being to drive them from the summit and from the windows so that the columns could rush the street and scale the redoubt by surprise, as on the evening before.

Enjolras ordered fire on the artillerymen. The long-silent barricade poured out seven or eight volleys with rage and joy, and when the smoke thinned two-thirds of the gunners lay beneath the wheels of the cannon; the survivors served the pieces with grave tranquillity, but the fire had slackened. Bossuet called it success. Enjolras shook his head: another quarter of an hour of this success and there would not be a cartridge left in the barricade. Gavroche, it appears, overheard him.

title: Gavroche Outside
summary: Gavroche slips out with a bottle basket to empty the cartridge boxes of the dead National Guardsmen in the street; under cover of the smoke he fills his basket, and when the soldiers begin shooting at him he stands up and sings back a couplet at every bullet, until one knocks him down and a second, as he sings on, kills him.
details: Courfeyrac saw someone at the foot of the barricade, outside in the street amid the bullets: Gavroche, with a bottle basket from the wine-shop, calmly emptying the cartridge boxes of the National Guardsmen killed on the slope. Told to come in, he answered "Instanter" and bounded further into the street, where Fannicot's company had left some twenty corpses, a provision of cartridges for the barricade. The smoke lay in the street like a fog, and thanks to it and his small size he rifled the first seven or eight boxes almost unseen, crawling on his belly, galloping on all fours, basket in his teeth, winding from body to body and opening each cartouche like a monkey opening a nut. On a corporal he found a powder-flask and pocketed it "for thirst." The insurgents dared not call him back for fear of drawing attention to him.

He went too far, to where the smoke thinned, and the sharpshooters behind their stone dike and the suburban guards at the corner pointed out something moving. A bullet struck the body he was robbing; a second struck sparks beside him; a third overturned his basket. Gavroche sprang to his feet, hands on hips, hair in the wind, and sang at the National Guardsmen that people were ugly at Nanterre and it was the fault of Voltaire, and stupid at Palaiseau and it was the fault of Rousseau. He picked up every fallen cartridge and went on plundering, answering each missed shot with a new couplet: he was not a notary, he was a little bird, joy was his character and misery his trousseau, all the fault of Voltaire and Rousseau. The soldiers laughed as they aimed, and always missed; he lay down, leapt up, hid in doorways, thumbed his nose at the grapeshot, a gamin-fairy, the invulnerable dwarf of the fray, while the barricade watched panting.

One bullet, better aimed or more treacherous, struck him at last. Gavroche staggered and sank, and the whole barricade cried out; but he rose to a sitting position, a thread of blood down his face, raised both arms towards where the shot had come from and began to sing that he had fallen to the ground, the fault of Voltaire, with his nose in the gutter, the fault of... He did not finish. A second bullet from the same marksman stopped him. He fell face down on the pavement and moved no more. That grand little soul had taken its flight.

title: How from a Brother One Becomes a Father
summary: At the same hour, in the deserted Luxembourg garden, the two lost little boys Gavroche once sheltered, the Thénardiers' sons, hide by the swans' hutch while a smug bourgeois lectures his sated son and throws his stale brioche to the swans; when they leave, the elder boy fishes the cake out of the basin and gives the larger half to his brother.
details: The drama's gaze shifts to the Luxembourg, closed by police order because of the insurrection and emptied of the troops that had bivouacked there. Two ragged children, about seven and five, were walking hand in hand on the sunny side of the paths, the elder leading with a little stick, the younger saying he was hungry. They were the two Gavroche had taken trouble over: children of the Thénardiers, leased to Magnon, attributed to M. Gillenormand, and now leaves blown from all those rootless branches, their once-clean clothes turned to rags. The locked gates had let them slip in and stay; the inspectors, more concerned with the outside than the inside, had not seen them.

Hugo gives the garden at eleven o'clock on the 6th of June its due: rain-washed foliage, lilies and carnations, tulips like flame, bees, the amorous old crows of Marie de Medici, the whole of nature breakfasting with not a beast's stomach empty. He pauses on the thinkers who are content with the infinite and forget to love, the magnificent egoists like Horace and Goethe who do not see the weeping child because the zodiac fills their eyes, great and pitiable at once; and he asks what there is above a sun that may be blind. The god.

The children had reached the great basin and hidden behind the swans' hutch when a bourgeois of about fifty arrived with his six-year-old son, who was dressed as a National Guardsman and carried a big brioche. Hugo suggests he was the same man Marius once overheard counselling his son to avoid excesses. The father, who walked like the swans and smiled because his mouth would not close, held forth on living content with little, called the distant firing the Saturnalia, and, catching sight of the two ragged boys, said that anarchy was entering the garden. His son was no longer hungry and found his cake stale; the father took it and flung it to the swans to teach compassion for animals, then, as the tumult grew sinister and a black cloud veiled the sun, hurried the boy home, saying the Tuileries were being attacked and that from the Tuileries to the Luxembourg was only the distance from royalty to the peerage.

As soon as they had gone the elder boy lay flat on the rim of the basin and reached out with his stick; the swans, hurrying towards the enemy, pushed a ripple before them that floated the brioche to his wand. He rapped it in, frightened the swans away, seized the wet cake, broke it into a large piece and a small one, kept the small one for himself, gave the large one to his brother and told him to ram it into his muzzle.

title: Mortuus Pater Filium Moriturum Expectat
summary: Marius and Combeferre run out too late; Marius carries Gavroche's body back, grazed by a bullet himself, and the child is laid beside Mabeuf under the black shawl; the cartridges give each man fifteen rounds, which Jean Valjean refuses, and the barricade waits in a strange calm.
details: Marius dashed out of the barricade with Combeferre behind him, but Gavroche was dead. Combeferre brought back the basket of cartridges; Marius carried the child, thinking that what Thénardier had done for his father he was now doing for Thénardier's son, except that Thénardier had brought back his father alive and he was bringing back the child dead. When he re-entered the redoubt his face, like Gavroche's, was covered in blood: a bullet had grazed his head as he stooped, and he had not noticed. Courfeyrac bandaged his brow with his cravat. They laid Gavroche on Mabeuf's table and spread the black shawl over both; there was enough of it for the old man and the child.

Combeferre distributed the cartridges, fifteen rounds a man. Jean Valjean, still motionless on his stone post, shook his head when offered his share. Combeferre called him a rare eccentric who found a way of not fighting in the barricade; Enjolras answered that this did not prevent him defending it, and Courfeyrac added that he was another sort from Father Mabeuf.

Hugo notes how little the bombardment disturbed the interior; men went and came, talked and jested, and the glow of heroism deepened as the position went from critical to menacing to desperate. Enjolras dominated it gravely; Combeferre in an apron dressed wounds; Bossuet and Feuilly made cartridges from the powder-flask Gavroche had taken from the dead corporal, Bossuet remarking that they would soon take the diligence for another planet; Courfeyrac laid out his arsenal of sword-cane, gun, two pistols and a cudgel; a workman tied Mother Hucheloup's straw hat on against sunstroke; Joly examined his tongue in the widow's mirror; some devoured mouldy crusts found in a drawer. Jean Valjean stared silently at the wall. Marius was troubled about what his father was going to say to him.

title: The Vulture Become Prey
summary: At noon the sappers appear at the head of the attacking column; Enjolras has the windows walled with stones and the bottles of aquafortis carried upstairs, gives his final orders to twenty-six men, and decrees that the last man to leave the taproom shall shoot Javert; Jean Valjean asks that privilege as his reward, Javert says it is just, and as the trumpets sound Javert tells the insurgents they will meet again shortly.
details: Hugo first insists that a barricade, whatever its inner calm, remains a vision to those inside it: one emerges from civil war as from a dream, with blood under one's nails and no clear memory. Then the clock struck midday, and before the twelve strokes ended Enjolras shouted for stones to be carried up to the windows and roofs: a squad of sappers with axes had appeared at the end of the street, the head of the assault column. In two minutes the spare paving-stones walled the first-floor window and the attic windows to half their height, with loopholes planned by Feuilly for the gun barrels; the two cannon were now firing ball at the centre of the barrier to open a breach. Enjolras had the fifteen bottles from under Mabeuf's table carried to the first floor. Asked who was to drink them, he said, "They." The lower window was blocked, the iron bars of the door made ready; the barricade was the rampart and the wine-shop the keep.

While the assailants made their preparations with irritating leisure, Enjolras reviewed everything, feeling that since such men were to die their death should be a masterpiece. He told Marius that they were the two leaders, that he would give the last orders inside and Marius should watch outside. He had the kitchen door nailed up so that the wounded would not be splashed, then gave his orders to Feuilly, who answered for all: axes ready on the first floor to cut the staircase, twenty-six men on foot, thirty-four guns, the eight spare ones kept loaded, twenty men to the barricade and six at the loopholes, all to rush to the barricade when the drum beat the assault.

Then he turned to Javert: "I am not forgetting you." He laid a pistol on the table and said the last man to leave the room should smash the spy's skull, not there, so as not to mix the corpses, but over the four-foot barricade in the Mondétour lane. Javert was more impassive than Enjolras himself. Here Jean Valjean stepped out of the group and asked whether the commander thought he deserved a recompense. Enjolras said the barricade had two saviours, Marius Pontmercy and himself. Valjean asked for one thing: to blow that man's brains out. Javert raised his head, saw him, made an almost imperceptible movement and said, "That is just." Enjolras, reloading, saw no objection and told him to take the spy. Valjean sat on the end of the table, took the pistol and cocked it. Almost at once trumpets sounded and Marius shouted a warning from the top of the barricade. Javert laughed his noiseless laugh, told the insurgents they were in no better case than he, and as they poured out at Enjolras's cry threw after them: "We shall meet again shortly!"

title: Jean Valjean Takes His Revenge
summary: Jean Valjean leads the bound Javert over the little Mondétour barricade, past Éponine's body, cuts his cords with a clasp-knife, tells him he lives as Fauchelevent at 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé and sends him away, then fires the pistol in the air and reports "It is done"; Marius, who has just recognised the prisoner as the Inspector Javert of the Rue de Pontoise, hears the shot with a chill.
details: Left alone with Javert, Jean Valjean untied the rope that bound him to the table and signed to him to rise. Javert obeyed with the smile of enchained authority. Valjean took him by the martingale like a beast by its breast-band and led him slowly, pistol in hand, across the inner court of the barricade; the insurgents, intent on the coming attack, had their backs turned, and only Marius, posted at the far left, saw the victim and executioner pass. Valjean made Javert climb the low entrenchment in the Mondétour lane, and they were alone. Among the heap of corpses lay a livid face with streaming hair, a pierced hand and a half-bare breast: Éponine. Javert glanced at it and said calmly that he thought he knew that girl.

Then Valjean put the pistol under his arm and fixed on Javert a look that needed no words: Javert, it is I. "Take your revenge," said Javert. Valjean drew a clasp-knife, and Javert remarked that it suited him better. But Valjean cut the martingale at his neck, the cords at his wrists and the cord at his feet, straightened up and said, "You are free." Javert, master of himself as he was, could not repress a start and stood open-mouthed. Valjean added that he did not expect to leave this place alive, but that if by chance he did, he lived under the name of Fauchelevent at No. 7, Rue de l'Homme Armé. Javert snarled like a tiger, muttered "Have a care," repeated the address and the number, buttoned his coat, folded his arms and walked off towards the Halles. A few minutes later he turned and shouted, "You annoy me. Kill me, rather," not noticing that he had stopped addressing Valjean as "thou." "Be off with you," said Valjean, and Javert turned the corner of the Rue des Prêcheurs. Valjean fired the pistol into the air, went back to the barricade and said, "It is done."

Meanwhile Marius, seeing the pinioned spy in daylight for the first time, had recognised him: the inspector of the Rue de Pontoise who had given him the two pistols he had used in this very barricade. The memory was misty, a question rather than a certainty, but perhaps there was still time to intervene. He called to Enjolras at the other end of the barricade and asked the police agent's name. "Javert." Marius sprang to his feet. At that moment the pistol shot rang out and Jean Valjean reappeared crying that it was done. A gloomy chill went through Marius's heart.

title: The Dead Are in the Right and the Living Are Not in the Wrong
summary: Before the final assault Hugo reflects on the closed houses that condemn the insurgents, on why a people abandons an uprising that comes too soon, on the guilt and grandeur of Utopia that takes up arms, on the distinction between accepted revolutions and refused riots, and on progress as the true subject of his book.
details: The death agony of the barricade was about to begin amid the splendour of the June day, the sobbing tocsin of Saint-Merry and the alarming silence of the houses. Since the evening before the two rows of houses in the Rue de la Chanvrerie had become walls. Hugo explains that when the moment is ripe the inhabitant becomes the combatant's ally and the house fraternises with the fortress; when the masses disown the movement the city turns to a desert, doors are nailed up, and the street becomes a defile that helps the army. Behind those shut doors families eat and sleep and are afraid; fear turns to fury, and the people inside say it is the insurgents' own fault and above all do not open. The wall has ears of flesh and the men bowels of stone. Whom to reproach? No one and everyone; the incomplete times.

Utopia that grows impatient and becomes revolt almost always comes too soon and must accept catastrophe in place of triumph. Is the people's abandonment ingratitude? Yes from the point of view of the human race, no from that of the individual, who has his own pardonable interests and his own short life. Hugo names progress as the permanent life of peoples and, recalling Gerard de Nerval's "God is dead, perhaps," insists that progress sleeps but always wakes taller. He adds a severe reservation: Utopia at war borrows battle from the lie of yesterday, shoots spies and executes traitors, and every blade has two edges. Even so he venerates the confessors of Utopia, most of all in failure, preferring martyrdom to success, John Brown to Washington.

There are accepted revolutions and refused revolutions called riots; an insurrection is an idea sitting its examination before the people. Peoples are positive and dislike insurrection because it ends in catastrophe and starts from an abstraction, yet it is always for the ideal that men sacrifice themselves. What the young men of the Rue de la Chanvrerie were fighting was not precisely Louis-Philippe, whom none of them hated, but the younger branch of divine right and, through it, the usurpation of man over man everywhere. Such men march with heads down hoping for victory and accepting Thermopylae. Hugo praises France as the artist among nations, the bearer of the torch after Greece and Italy, warns against both dogma and lucre, grants peoples the right to an eclipse, and insists that the stomach must not be the sole wisdom.

He ends by naming his book's subject. The battle he is describing is a convulsion towards the ideal, an epilepsy of trammelled progress. The whole work, from end to end, is the march from evil to good, from night to day, from appetite to conscience, from nothingness to God: matter at the point of departure, the soul at the point of arrival; the hydra at the beginning, the angel at the end.

title: The Heroes
summary: The drum beats the charge and the army hurls itself on the barricade, which holds through ten assaults in a battle like a wall of Troy; Enjolras fights sheltered and untouched, Marius exposed and streaming with blood, and Bossuet, Feuilly, Courfeyrac and Combeferre are killed.
details: The attack came as a hurricane. In broad daylight, surprise impossible, a powerful column of the line interspersed with National and Municipal Guard, with sappers at its head and drums and trumpets sounding, charged straight at the barricade with the weight of a brazen beam. The wall held. For a moment it was flooded with assailants, then shook them off as a lion shakes off dogs, and the repulsed column, massed in the street, answered with a horizontal bouquet of musketry that picked off men one after another. On both sides the bravery was almost barbarous; National Guardsmen fought like Zouaves, and the street was strewn with corpses.

Enjolras held one end of the barricade and Marius the other. Enjolras, who carried the whole defence in his head, sheltered himself, and three soldiers fell under his embrasure without seeing him; Marius fought unprotected, more than half his body above the breastwork, formidable and pensive, a phantom firing a gun. The cartridges were giving out but not the sarcasms. Courfeyrac, bareheaded, said the cannonballs had finally taken his hat; Feuilly bitterly named the well-known men who had sworn to join them and had abandoned them, and Combeferre answered that some people observe honour as one observes the stars, from a great distance. The interior was so strewn with torn cartridges that it looked like snow.

The attackers had numbers, the insurgents position, and the army closed in step by step like a vice. Assault followed assault. These ragged, starving, sleepless men, nearly all wounded, with a few rounds left and notched swords, became Titans, and the barricade was ten times attacked, scaled and never captured; Hugo compares it to the Forest of Swords of the Veda and renounces any attempt to depict the whole slaughter. They fought hand to hand from roofs, windows and cellar gratings, one against sixty, and the façade of Corinthe was half demolished.

Bossuet was killed; Feuilly was killed; Courfeyrac was killed; Combeferre, pierced by three bayonet thrusts in the breast as he lifted a wounded soldier, had only time to glance at heaven before he died. Marius, still fighting, was so riddled with wounds, especially in the head, that his face vanished under blood. Enjolras alone was untouched; when he had no weapon left, a hand thrust some arm into his fist, and all he had were the stumps of four swords. Hugo closes with Homer's roll of the slain and the old frescoes of iron-clad dukes, and insists that a peasant recruit and a pale student, each believing he fights for his country, cast a shadow in the epic field of humanity as long as any Ajax.

title: Foot to Foot
summary: With only Enjolras and Marius left of the leaders, the centre gives way and the final assault carries the barricade; Enjolras holds the wine-shop door alone to let the survivors in, Marius falls outside with a broken collarbone and feels an unknown hand seize him, and the besieged fight on from the first floor with their last cartridges and bottles of aquafortis.
details: When no leader was left alive but Enjolras and Marius at the two ends, the centre that Courfeyrac, Joly, Bossuet, Feuilly and Combeferre had so long sustained gave way. The cannon had hollowed the middle of the redoubt into two slopes, the outer one an inclined plane for attack, and a last assault up it succeeded; the bayonets came over the crest through the smoke and the defenders of the centre fell back in confusion. Then the love of life woke in some of them: hemmed in by the six-storey house at the back of the redoubt, they battered at its door with gun-butts and kicks, begging to be let in. No one opened. From the third-floor window the dead man's head looked down on them.

Enjolras and Marius and the seven or eight rallied round them sprang to protect these men. Enjolras shouted to the soldiers not to advance, and when an officer disobeyed he killed him. Then, back against the Corinthe building, sword in one hand and rifle in the other, he held the wine-shop door open, shielding the fugitives with his body against an entire battalion, whirling his rifle like a singlestick round his head, and was the last in. The door slammed so violently that it left five fingers of a soldier who had clung to it glued to the post.

Marius stayed outside. A shot had broken his collarbone; he felt himself fainting and falling, and with his eyes already shut felt a vigorous hand seize him, having only time to think, with a last memory of Cosette, that he was taken prisoner and would be shot. Enjolras, not seeing Marius among those in the wine-shop, thought the same, but there was no time; he barred, bolted and chained the door while muskets and sappers' axes beat on it. The soldiers were full of rage, both for the dead artillery sergeant and because of a false rumour that the insurgents had been mutilating prisoners and had a headless soldier in the wine-shop.

Enjolras said, "Let us sell our lives dearly," then bent over the table where Mabeuf and Gavroche lay under the black cloth and kissed the old man's hand that hung to the floor, as he had kissed his brow the evening before, the only two kisses of his life. Hugo abridges: the barricade had fought like a gate of Thebes, the wine-shop fought like a house of Saragossa. Paving-stones rained from the windows and roof; when the door yielded the assailants found no one alive below, the staircase cut down with axes, and a terrific fire pouring through the hole in the ceiling: the last cartridges. When those were gone, each man on the first floor took two of the reserved bottles and held the scaling party off with these fragile clubs. They were bottles of aquafortis. It resembled Milton and Dante rather than Homer; demons attacked and spectres resisted. It was heroism become monstrous.

title: Orestes Fasting and Pylades Drunk
summary: The assailants break into the first floor and find only Enjolras on his feet; he offers his breast to a firing squad, and Grantaire, waking from his drunken sleep, declares himself one of them and asks to be shot with him; Enjolras presses his hand with a smile, and both fall; the last insurgents are killed in the attic and cellar, and the barricade is taken.
details: Climbing on each other's backs, up the skeleton of the staircase and the walls, a score of soldiers and guardsmen, most of them disfigured by wounds and blind with blood, burst into the first-floor room. Only one man was still standing: Enjolras, without cartridges or sword, holding the barrel of his gun whose stock he had broken on the heads of the first to enter, the billiard table between him and his attackers, head high in a corner, still so alarming that a space emptied round him. They cried that this was the leader who had killed the artilleryman and that he should be shot where he stood. "Shoot me," said Enjolras, and threw away his stump of gun-barrel, folded his arms and offered his breast.

The audacity of a fine death stilled the room. Enjolras, bloody but unwounded, fresh and rosy after twenty-four hours of combat, seemed to compel his killers to kill him respectfully; a witness later spoke of an insurgent they called Apollo, and one guardsman lowered his gun, saying it seemed to him he was about to shoot a flower. Twelve men formed a squad opposite him, a sergeant shouted the aim, and an officer intervened to ask whether he wished his eyes bandaged. "No." Was it he who had killed the artillery sergeant? "Yes."

Grantaire had woken a few moments before. He had been dead drunk in that upper room since the evening before, head on his arms among the glasses and bottles, snoring through fusillade, cannonballs and assault, so like the corpses around him that no one had noticed him; noise does not rouse a drunkard, silence does, and the sudden halt of the tumult woke him. His intoxication tore away like a curtain and he understood everything at once. As the sergeant was about to repeat the order, a strong voice beside the soldiers shouted, "Long live the Republic! I'm one of them." Grantaire crossed the room with a firm stride, placed himself before the guns beside Enjolras and said, "Finish both of us at one blow." Then, gently, to Enjolras: "Do you permit it?" Enjolras pressed his hand with a smile.

The smile had not ended when the volley sounded. Enjolras, pierced by eight bullets, remained leaning against the wall as though nailed there, his head bowed. Grantaire fell at his feet as if struck by a thunderbolt. A few moments later the soldiers dislodged the last insurgents from the top of the house, firing into the attic, flinging bodies still alive from the windows; two light-infantrymen were shot lifting the omnibus, a soldier and an insurgent fell from the roof locked together, and a similar struggle ended in the cellar. Then silence. The barricade was captured, and the soldiers began to search the houses round about and pursue the fugitives.

title: Prisoner
summary: The hand that seized Marius was Jean Valjean's: having fought only by rescuing the wounded, he carried the unconscious Marius into the sheltered angle where Éponine died, and, trapped between the massacre and a guarded barricade, found an iron grating under the loose paving-stones, lifted it, and descended with Marius on his shoulders into a long, silent underground corridor.
details: Marius was indeed a prisoner, but the hand that gripped him as he fell was Jean Valjean's. Valjean had taken no part in the fighting except to expose himself in it; thanks to him, everywhere present like a providence, the fallen had been picked up, carried to the taproom and cared for, and no blow or attack or even act of self-defence came from his hands. He received only a few scratches; the bullets would have none of him. Hugo doubts he had come there to seek suicide, an irreligious act. He had seemed not to see Marius and had never taken his eyes off him; when the shot laid Marius low, Valjean leapt on him like a tiger on its prey and bore him off, and in the fury concentrated on Enjolras and the wine-shop door no one saw him cross the barricade and disappear behind the angle of the Corinthe building.

That angle made a little cape sheltered from bullets and eyes, the fold in which Éponine had breathed her last. Valjean set Marius down against the wall and looked about him. For a moment or two the spot was safe, but the implacable house in front of him was shut, the low barricade on his right towards the Rue de la Petite Truanderie had a line of bayonets behind it that would greet any head with sixty shots, and on his left was the battle; if a single soldier turned the corner, all was over. He remembered his escape from the Rue Polonceau eight years before; that had been difficult, this was impossible. Only a bird could have got out.

Staring at the ground as though to pierce a hole in it with his eyes, he made out at the base of the little barricade, under a disordered heap of paving-stones, an iron grating about two feet square, lying flat and loosened from its frame, with a dark shaft below it like a chimney flue or a cistern pipe. His old art of escape rose in him like an illumination. He thrust aside the stones, raised the grating, lifted the inert Marius onto his shoulders, climbed down with elbows and knees into the well, let the heavy trap fall back with the stones rolling over it, and stood on a flagged floor three metres down, all in a few minutes, with the strength of a giant and the speed of an eagle.

He found himself with the unconscious Marius in a long underground corridor of profound peace, absolute silence and night. The feeling of his fall into the convent garden came back to him, only what he carried now was not Cosette but Marius. The tumult of the wine-shop taken by assault reached him overhead only as a vague murmur.

title: The Land Impoverished by the Sea
summary: Opening his book on the sewers, Hugo argues that Paris throws twenty-five million francs a year into the river in the form of human manure that should fertilise the fields, that the sewer is an economic mistake Rome made before Paris, and that beneath the city of light lies Lutetia, the city of mud, a colossal sponge of galleries whose offspring is the rat.
details: Hugo begins with an accountant's thesis: Paris casts twenty-five millions a year into the water, without metaphor, by means of its intestine, the sewer. Science now knows that human manure is the richest fertiliser; the Chinese have always known it, and their soil is as young as in Abraham's day. Fleets go to the South Pole for the dung of petrels while the detritus of a capital, which could feed the world if returned to the land, is swept into the abyss. The filth carted through the streets at night is in truth the flowering meadow, the cattle, the golden wheat, the bread on the table and the blood in the veins.

France alone, he says, deposits half a milliard a year in the Atlantic through its rivers, a quarter of the budget, with two results: the land impoverished and the water poisoned, hunger from the furrow and disease from the stream; the Thames is poisoning London, and Paris has had to move its sewer mouths below the last bridge. A simple double system of pipes, already working in English towns, would bring the fields' pure water to the city and send the city's rich water back to the fields. The sewer is a mistake; drainage that restores what it takes would increase the earth's yield tenfold and lighten the problem of misery. Paris, the model city, is a spendthrift, and in this it imitates Rome, whose sewer, as Liebig says, absorbed the well-being of the Roman peasant and then engulfed Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and Africa.

For this operation Paris has beneath it another Paris of sewers, with its streets, crossroads, squares and blind alleys, a circulation of mire without the human form. If Paris contains Athens, Tyre, Sparta and Nineveh, it also contains Lutetia, the city of mud, a grandiose vileness like Machiavelli or Mirabeau among men. The subsoil, apart from catacombs, gas pipes and water mains, is a colossal madrepore, a shadowy labyrinth under both banks whose only guiding thread is its slope. In its humid mist appears the rat, the creature Paris seems to have given birth to.

title: Ancient History of the Sewer
summary: Hugo sketches the sewer network as a branch grafted on the river and an alphabet of misshapen letters, recalls how sewers have served as sepulchre and asylum for outlaws and persecuted thought through the centuries, and calls the sewer the conscience of the city, the one place where nothing lies and where history's murderers are still scrubbing at their traces.
details: Seen from above with Paris lifted off like a lid, the sewers would outline a great branch grafted on the river, the belt sewer its trunk and the dead-end ducts its twigs, though Hugo prefers the image of an eccentric oriental alphabet, misshapen letters welded together at random against a background of shadow. Sinks and sewers were objects of almost religious dread in antiquity and the Middle Ages, from the vermin ditch of Benares to the sink of Nineveh; false prophets drew their false moons and suns from cesspools.

The history of men is reflected in the history of sewers. The Paris sewer has been a sepulchre and an asylum: crime, intelligence, social protest, liberty of conscience, thought and theft, everything the law has persecuted, has hidden there, the Maillotins in the fourteenth century, the Huguenots in the sixteenth, the chauffeurs in the eighteenth. A hundred years ago the pickpocket in danger slipped into it as into a bedroom; the forest had its cave and Paris its sewer, where Villon within converses with Rabelais without.

The sewer, Hugo says, is the conscience of the city, where everything converges and nothing keeps a secret. Filth does not lie: there the bottle-end confesses drunkenness, the apple-core that had literary opinions becomes an apple-core again, the gaming-house louis jostles the suicide's nail, a foetus rolls in last Shrove Tuesday's spangles. All that was rouged is washed clean; a sewer is a cynic and tells everything, and its sincerity rests the soul after the great airs of reasons of state and incorruptible robes. History too passes through it: the Saint Bartholomews filter through its stones drop by drop, and the thinker sees Louis XI with Tristan, Charles IX with his mother, Richelieu with Louis XIII, kneeling in its gloom with a scrap of shroud for an apron, sponging out their work. The social observer must enter these shadows; philosophy, the microscope of thought, reconstructs the city from the cesspool as it infers the amphora from the potsherd.

title: Bruneseau
summary: Hugo recounts the sewer's legendary past, the inundations when the cesspool flowed back into the city, notably in 1802, and the terror that kept even the police from exploring it, until in 1805 the Minister of the Interior told Napoleon he had met the most intrepid man in the Empire, a man who wanted to visit the sewers of Paris: Bruneseau.
details: The medieval sewer of Paris was legendary; Henri II attempted a survey in the sixteenth century and failed, and a hundred years ago the cesspool was simply left to itself. Old Paris, Hugo says, had not much head, and could no more sweep out filth than abuses; above the unintelligible city lay the inextricable sewer, Daedalus backing up Babel. Sometimes the sewer overflowed like an enraged Nile, and the city tasted its own filth, a resemblance to remorse that served as a warning badly received. The inundation of 1802, still remembered by Parisians of eighty, spread mud over the Place des Victoires and into the Rue Saint-Honoré, reached three feet in the Rue Saint-Pierre, and on the left bank stopped a few paces from the house where Racine had lived.

At the start of the century the sewer was still a place of mystery and terror. Paris knew in a confused way that it had a cavern beneath it, talked of as of the monstrous bed of Thebes; sewermen's boots never went beyond certain known points; carts were tipped straight into it and cleaning was left to the rain. Rome had called its sewer the Gemoniae, Paris called hers the Polypus-Hole. Hygiene and legend agreed in horror: the goblin bred under the Mouffetard sewer, the fever of 1685 was blamed on the gaping hiatus of the Marais sewer, and the toothed grating of the Rue de la Mortellerie breathed hell like a dragon's maw. The sewer had no bottom; it was the lower world, and not even the police thought of exploring it. Yet the cesspool found its Christopher Columbus.

One day in 1805, during one of the Emperor's rare appearances in Paris, with the veterans of the Rhine, the Nile and Lodi crowding the Carrousel in that splendid moment between Marengo and Austerlitz, the Minister of the Interior told Napoleon at his levee that he had seen the most intrepid man in his Empire the day before. What had he done? He wanted to do something: to visit the sewers of Paris. This man existed and his name was Bruneseau.

title: Details Ignored
summary: Bruneseau's seven-year exploration of the sewers, from 1805 to 1812, is a nocturnal campaign against pestilence in which eight of twenty labourers refuse at the outset, men faint and vanish into bottomless holes, dated stones mark the work of past centuries, and the strangest finds are an orangutan's skeleton and a rag of fine batiste hanging from a hinge: a morsel of Marat's shroud.
details: The visit was a formidable campaign, a night battle against suffocation and a voyage of discovery; one young workman who survived it later told the details Bruneseau left out of his official report. Eight of his twenty labourers refused to go further at the first turnings. The work was double: to cleanse and to survey at once, noting inflows, counting gratings and vents, mapping branches, sounding side-drains and measuring every vault. Lanterns pined in the foul air, fainting sewermen were carried out, the floor gave way into bottomless wells and one man vanished and was got out with difficulty; on Fourcroy's advice they burned cages of resinous tow where the air had been cleared, and in places the stone itself seemed diseased with misshapen fungi.

Going downhill, Bruneseau read on a stone at the Grand-Hurleur the date 1550, where Philibert Delorme's survey for Henri II had halted; he found seventeenth-century vaulting in the Ponceau drain and eighteenth-century work of 1740 in the collector, both more cracked than the belt sewer of 1412, when the brook of Ménilmontant was raised to the dignity of the Grand Sewer. Under the Courthouse they thought they recognised ancient dungeons cut into the sewer itself, with an iron collar still hanging in one, and walled them up. They found a perfectly preserved ragpicker's basket, jewels, coins, a Huguenot medal of a pig in a cardinal's hat, and the skeleton of an orangutan that had vanished from the Jardin des Plantes in 1800, probably the devil who had appeared in the Rue des Bernardins.

The most surprising encounter was at the entrance to the Grand Sewer, where a shapeless rag hung from the hinge of a vanished grating. It was very fine batiste, and in one corner they made out a marquis's coronet and the letters LAVBESP: Laubespine. It was a piece of Marat's shroud, the sheet he had kept from a youthful love affair with a great lady when he was physician to the Comte d'Artois's stables, and the only fine linen in his house when he died; old women had wrapped him in it, and it had passed through the Pantheon to end with the rats. They left it hanging, from scorn or respect, both of which Marat deserved.

The whole visit lasted seven years, from 1805 to 1812, and as he went Bruneseau built: lowering the Ponceau arch in 1808, pushing the sewer under the Rue Saint-Denis in 1809, under the Salpêtrière in 1810, the Place Royale in 1811, the Rue de la Paix in 1812, disinfecting the whole network and taking on his son-in-law Nargaud in the second year. Thus old society performed the toilet of its double bottom. Hugo closes with a portrait of the antique sewer as it had been: tortuous, cracked, unpaved, fetid and wild, a titanic mole-burrow where the past prowls blindly in the filth that was once splendour.

title: Present Progress
summary: Today's sewer, Hugo says, is clean, cold, straight and almost respectable, a tradesman turned councillor of state, though it still exhales a suspicious odour like Tartuffe after confession; the revolution between the old sewer and the new was the work of the man everyone forgets, Bruneseau.
details: The modern sewer is clean, cold, straight and correct, almost what the English call respectable; it is proper and greyish, laid out by rule and line, like a tradesman who has become a councillor of state. The mire there behaves with decency. One might mistake it for one of those underground corridors so useful to fleeing kings in the good old days; the classical alexandrine, driven out of poetry, seems to have taken refuge in its long whitish vault, and even the Rue de Rivoli serves as a pattern underground. The administrative vocabulary has grown dignified: what was a gut is a gallery, what was a hole is a surveying orifice. Villon would no longer find his old lodging there.

Its immemorial population of rats swarms more than ever, but even they grow tame in their subterranean palace, and the rain that once soiled the sewer now washes it. Yet one should not trust it too far: miasmas still live there, and for all the efforts of the prefecture and the health commission it exhales a vague, suspicious odour, like Tartuffe after confession. Still, Tartuffe's conscience is an advance on the Augean stables, and the sweeping is a homage the sewer pays to civilisation.
It is more than progress; it is transmutation, a revolution between the ancient and the present sewer. And the man who effected it is the man everyone forgets, whom Hugo has just named: Bruneseau.

title: Future Progress
summary: Hugo tallies the growth of the sewers from twenty-three thousand metres in 1806 to sixty leagues today, describes the rebellious soil, floods, quicksands and typhus that killed the engineers who built them, notes that in 1832 much of the old gothic sewer still gaped in the streets, and returns to his theme that washing the sewer back onto the fields would diminish misery and disease.
details: The sewer grows with Paris, a polyp stretching out an arm every time the city cuts a street. The old monarchy had built twenty-three thousand three hundred metres by 1806; Napoleon added under five thousand, Louis XVIII nearly six, Charles X nearly eleven, Louis-Philippe eighty-nine thousand, the Republic of 1848 twenty-three thousand, the present government seventy thousand: in all two hundred and twenty-six thousand metres, sixty leagues, more than ten times what existed at the century's start. The soil of Paris resists the pick: liquid clays, springs, hard rock and the deep quagmires called moutardes; rivulets burst into half-built vaults, marl rolls down like a cataract, quicksands at Belleville swallow a man visibly, and typhus slowly impregnates the workmen. Hugo names the superintendent Monnot, who died after building the sewer from the Barrière Blanche to Aubervilliers in four months of day-and-night work, and the engineer Duleau, who died after vaulting three thousand metres across the city; there are no bulletins for such bravery, more useful than that of the battlefield.

The sewers of 1832 were far from today's. Bruneseau had given the impulse, but it took the cholera to force the great reconstruction. In 1821 part of the belt sewer still lay open to the sky in the Rue des Gourdes, and the absorbing wells only date from 1836. At the time of the insurrection of the 5th and 6th of June many streets were still sunken causeways with heavy square gratings, called cassis, polished and slippery under horses' hooves, and in a long list of streets, from the Rue du Temple to the Champs-Élysées and the Rue de Tournon, the old gothic sewer still displayed its maw with monumental effrontery. From 1806 to 1831 some seven hundred and fifty metres a year were built; since then eight to ten thousand a year, in small stone and hydraulic mortar at two hundred francs the metre.

Beyond economics lie questions of public health. Paris sits between a sheet of water, pure and fed by the Seine, Marne, Yonne and Loire oozing through the green clay beneath the chalk, and a sheet of air that comes from the sewer and is unhealthy; the air above a dung-heap is purer than the air above Paris, and disease radiates fifty leagues around the Louvre. In time the sheet of water will be used to wash the sewer, by which Hugo means restoring the filth to the soil, and the whole community will gain in health and lose in misery. For ten centuries the cesspool has been the disease of Paris, held in a horror like the knacker's trade; the proverb said that to descend into the sewer was to enter the grave, and the sink bears the traces of every cataclysm from the shells of the Deluge to the rag of Marat.

title: The Sewer and Its Surprises
summary: Jean Valjean, carrying the bleeding Marius through the dark sewer, turns away from the Seine outlets that would deliver him into the crowded centre of Paris, climbs the Montmartre sewer without knowing where he is, passes the watershed and heads towards the belt sewer, until he sees his own shadow thrown ahead of him by a lantern: a police patrol is behind him.
details: In the heart of the city Jean Valjean had escaped from the city, passing in the time it took to lift and replace a grating from midday to midnight and from the whirlwind of murder to the stagnation of the tomb; the waste-trap of safety had opened beneath him, an adorable ambush of providence. He stood blind and deaf for a moment, not knowing whether the man on his shoulders was alive or a corpse, then felt the narrow walls and the wet floor and smelt where he was. When his eyes adjusted he saw that the passage behind him was walled up, a blind branch, and that the faint light from the manhole died a dozen paces ahead. The soldiers might notice the grating too, so there was not a minute to lose; he hoisted Marius again and plunged into the dark.

After fifty paces he met a cross passage and had to choose. The labyrinth's clue is its slope: to follow it is to reach the river. He reasoned that he was probably in the sewer of the Halles, and that to go left and downhill would bring him in a quarter of an hour to some mouth on the Seine between the Pont au Change and the Pont-Neuf, two bleeding men emerging from the ground in the most crowded spot in Paris, to be seized at once. He climbed the incline and turned right instead. Marius's arms were round his neck and his feet dragged; his cheek clung to Valjean's, bleeding, and a warm breath at Valjean's ear told him he was alive. The rain of the day before ran in a little torrent down the middle, so he hugged the wall.

Hugo lays out what Valjean did not know. He thought he was under the Rue Saint-Denis, whose old stone sewer runs straight to the Grand Sewer; in fact the gut of the Petite-Truanderie led into the Montmartre sewer, one of the most labyrinthine of the old network, with the Plâtrière sewer on his left like a Chinese puzzle, the three-toothed Rue du Cadran gallery on his right, the zigzag branch of the Mail and the dead end of the Rue des Jeûneurs between him and the belt sewer, the only way to a safe distant outlet. Had he known, the cheap porous stone under his hand would have told him he was not under the Rue Saint-Denis. Horror seized him by degrees as he walked in an enigma, asking whether Marius would die of haemorrhage and he of hunger, two skeletons in a corner of the night; like the prophet, he was in the belly of the monster. Then the water began to beat his heels instead of his toes: the sewer was descending. He feared he was going to the Seine, but he had in fact crossed the watershed and was heading for the belt sewer, on the right path without knowing it. At every branch he felt the angles and avoided any opening narrower than his own passage, judging rightly that it must be a dead end, and so escaped the fourfold trap.

He heard a distant continuous thunder overhead, the rumbling of vehicles: he was passing from the Paris petrified by the uprising into the living city. He had walked half an hour, only shifting Marius from hand to hand, when suddenly he saw his own shadow ahead of him on a faint reddish glow that gilded the viscous walls. He turned. Far behind him, piercing the dark, flamed a horrible star that seemed to be watching him, and behind it eight or ten black upright forms moved confusedly. It was the gloomy star of the police rising in the sewer.

title: Explanation
summary: A police patrol searching the sewers for fugitive insurgents has heard Valjean's footsteps; he freezes against the wall, the patrol listens, hears nothing, decides to hurry towards Saint-Merry instead of wasting time in the belt sewer, and the sergeant fires one shot into the dark that strikes the arch above Valjean's head before the lantern disappears.
details: On the 6th of June a battue of the sewers had been ordered: while General Bugeaud swept public Paris, Prefect Gisquet was to search the occult city for vanquished insurgents who might have taken refuge there. Three squads of agents and sewermen, armed with carbines, bludgeons, swords and poniards, explored the right bank, the left bank and the Cité. The lantern aimed at Jean Valjean belonged to the right-bank patrol, which had just searched the curving gallery and the three blind alleys under the Rue du Cadran, the very opening Valjean had passed by because it was narrower than his passage. Emerging, the police thought they heard footsteps towards the belt sewer, and the sergeant raised his lantern.

It was an indescribable moment for Valjean, but if he saw the lantern well, the lantern saw him badly: it was light and he was shadow, far off and mingled with the dark.
