He hugged the wall and stopped, and when he stopped the sound stopped. Half-visionary from hunger and sleeplessness, he did not understand what the gleam and the forms behind him were. The patrol listened and heard nothing, looked and saw nothing, and gathered in a circle at a service crossroads of the Montmartre sewer, where Valjean saw the bulldog heads whispering together. They concluded they had been mistaken, that it was useless to get tangled in the belt sewer, and that any "bousingot" to be hunted was towards Saint-Merry. The sergeant ordered a turn to the left, towards the Seine. Had they split into two squads, Valjean would have been taken; the prefecture's instructions, anticipating insurgents in force, had probably forbidden it. All hung on that thread.

Before leaving, to satisfy his policeman's conscience, the sergeant fired his gun in Valjean's direction. The detonation rolled from echo to echo through the crypt, and a fragment of plaster splashing into the stream a few paces from Valjean told him the ball had struck the vault over his head. Measured steps died away along the timber-work, the reddish glow faded, blindness and deafness resumed possession of the shadows, and Valjean, not daring to stir, stayed a long time leaning on the wall with straining ears and dilated pupils, watching the phantom patrol vanish.

title: The “Spun” Man
summary: That same afternoon, on the deserted right bank of the Seine beyond the Pont des Invalides, a man in rags is being quietly "spun" by a buttoned-up man of authority who has signalled a hackney-coach to follow; the fugitive walks to the dead end of the shore, vanishes behind a heap of rubbish, and the pursuer finds only a locked sewer grating that has just been opened with a key.
details: Hugo credits the police of that period with never letting a revolt distract them from ordinary duty: on the afternoon of the 6th of June, under the pressure of a possible revolution, an agent was still "spinning" a thief. On the slope of the right bank a little beyond the Pont des Invalides, where there is no longer any shore today, two men walked some distance apart, the one in front trying to get away without seeming to, the one behind trying to overtake him without hurrying, like a game of checkers played at a distance. Seen from the opposite quay, the first was a bristling, tattered, equivocal figure in a ragged blouse, furious as well as afraid; the second a classic, official personage in the frock-coat of authority buttoned to the chin. Hugo hints that the reader might recognise them at closer range, but does not name them.

The pursuer's object, Hugo suggests, was to clothe the first man more warmly, in red rather than blue; if he had not yet seized him, it was in the hope of being led to some meeting-place and some group worth catching, the delicate operation called spinning. Seeing an empty hackney-coach pass on the quay above, he made a sign, and the driver, who evidently knew with whom he was dealing, turned and followed the two men at a walking pace; the police instruct their agents always to have a coach on hand. The man in the blouse, to his follower's surprise, did not take the watering ramp up to the Champs-Élysées but kept on along the bank, which narrowed towards the Pont de Jéna into a tongue that ended in the water, blocked by the quay wall on one side and the river on the other, with only a heap of demolition rubbish six or seven feet high to hide the end.

The fugitive went round the heap and was lost to sight; the pursuer, no longer seen, walked fast, rounded it in his turn, and stopped in amazement. The man was gone. The shore ran only thirty paces further into the water, and no one could have jumped into the Seine unseen. Then he struck his brow: where the land met the water was a large, low, arched iron grating with a heavy lock and three massive hinges, a door at the base of the quay through which a blackish stream ran into the river. Beyond its rusty bars a dark vaulted corridor could be made out. He shook it; it held firm. It had evidently just been opened, silently, and closed again, which meant the man had not a hook but a key. "That is too much! A government key!" he exclaimed, then composed himself with a string of ironic monosyllables and settled behind the rubbish to watch with the patient rage of a pointer, while the coach halted on the quay above and its driver put the oat-bags on his horses, and passers-by on the Pont de Jéna glanced at the two motionless items in the landscape.

title: He Also Bears His Cross
summary: Bent double under Marius, thirsty, bitten by rats and failing, Valjean reaches the Grand Sewer about three in the afternoon, chooses rightly to go downstream, and at an air-hole lays Marius down, binds his wounds with his own shirt, eats the roll in his pocket and reads the note in his pocketbook naming M. Gillenormand, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, before carrying him on into deepening darkness.
details: Valjean resumed his march and the going grew harder. The vaults averaged five and a half feet, so he had to bend at every step to keep Marius's head from the stone and rise again, groping along walls too slimy to hold. The gleams from the air-holes were rare and so wan that full sunlight looked like moonlight. He was hungry and above all thirsty, in a place full of water where a man cannot drink; his prodigious strength, little diminished by age thanks to his chaste and sober life, began to give way, and Marius, perhaps dead, grew heavier as it ebbed. Rats slid between his legs and one bit him. About three in the afternoon he reached the belt sewer and was astonished by the sudden width: eight feet by seven, a gallery where his outstretched hands could not touch both walls.

At the junction with the galleries of the Rue de Provence and the Abattoir he chose the broadest passage, the belt sewer, and, judging that he must reach the Seine at any risk, turned left to descend. Hugo explains that this saved him: the Grand Sewer, the old brook of Ménilmontant, ends upstream in a blind sack at its source, and had he climbed it he would have died at a wall; only a man who knew the whole madrepore could have reached the Amelot outlet by the Filles-du-Calvaire passage. Asked where he was, Valjean would have answered, "In the night." His instinct served him. He passed the claw-shaped branches under the Rue Laffitte and the Rue Saint-Georges and the long corridor of the Chaussée d'Antin.

A little beyond the Madeleine branch, under a large air-hole, probably in the Rue d'Anjou, he halted, exhausted, and laid Marius down on the banquette with the gentleness of a brother. Under the wan light Marius's face was like ashes at the bottom of a tomb, his eyes closed, his hair plastered red, his hands limp, blood clotted in his cravat and at the corners of his mouth, his coat chafing the open gashes. Valjean laid a hand on his breast: the heart still beat. He tore up his shirt, bound the wounds as best he could and stopped the bleeding, then, bending over the unconscious young man in that half light, gazed at him with inexpressible hatred.

In Marius's pockets he had found the roll forgotten there the evening before and his pocketbook. He ate the roll and opened the book to the lines Marius had written: that his name was Marius Pontmercy and his body should be carried to his grandfather, M. Gillenormand, No. 6 Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, in the Marais. He read them by the air-hole, repeated the address in a low voice, put the book back, and, his strength restored, took Marius on his back again with his head on his right shoulder. Hugo notes that the torch of street names lighting this march for the reader was one Valjean did not possess; only the paling light and the thinning rumble of vehicles told him that evening was coming and that he was leaving central Paris for some solitary region near the outer quays. The air-holes grew fewer and the gloom deepened. Suddenly the darkness became terrible.

title: In the Case of Sand as in That of Woman, There Is a Fineness Which Is Treacherous
summary: Valjean feels the pavement turn to mud beneath him, and Hugo breaks off to describe the quicksands of Breton and Scottish beaches and their underground equivalent in the old sewers, the fontis, a slough into which sewermen and even a young vicomte had vanished, death in the mire being the one death that is not merely sinister but deformed.
details: He felt that he was entering water and that there was no longer pavement under his feet, only mud. Hugo turns to the beaches of Brittany and Scotland where a traveller walking at low tide notices that the sand has become birdlime and that each footprint fills with water, sinks in two or three inches, tries to turn back and sinks deeper, and recognises with terror that he is caught in a quicksand. He flings away his burden too late; he shouts and waves his hat; if the beach is deserted he is condemned to a long, implacable burial that drags him down by the feet while leaving him time to see the horizon, the villages, the sails and the birds, until the sand reaches his belly, his breast, his throat, fills his shouting mouth and closes his eyes, and a hand pierces the surface, waves and disappears. The earth, permeated with the ocean, drowns a man.

This fate was possible thirty years ago in the sewers of Paris. Before the works of 1833, water seeping into friable strata dissolved the underpinning of the flagged or cemented floor, which cracked and crumbled, and the gulf of mire so formed was called a fontis: the quicksand of Mont Saint-Michel inside a sewer, neither earth nor water, sometimes three or four feet deep, sometimes bottomless. If water predominated death was quick, if earth, slow. Hugo makes the reader picture it: instead of open sky and the hope of passers-by, deafness, blindness, a black vault, slow suffocation by filth with the whole city unaware overhead. Death on a pyre or in a shipwreck can be great; death in mire is filthy and humiliating, and the dying man does not know whether he is becoming a spectre or a frog. Everywhere else the sepulchre is sinister; here it is deformed.

Fontis varied with the subsoil: a man would take a day to disappear in the Lunière fontis and five minutes in the Philippeaux slough; a child could escape where a man perished, and the first law of safety was to throw off every load, which is why a sewerman who felt the ground yield dropped his tools first. They were caused by friable soil, deep slips, summer downpours, winter floods and the weight of houses forcing out the vaults; sometimes a saw-toothed gap between paving-stones betrayed the break above, often nothing did, and woe to the sewermen then. The registers name the drowned, among them Blaise Poutrain under the Rue Carême-Prenant, brother of the last gravedigger of the Innocents, and the young Vicomte d'Escoubleau, a hero of Lérida, who, surprised one night at his cousin the Duchesse de Sourdis's, took refuge from the Duke in the Beautreillis sewer and was swallowed; Madame de Sourdis, told of his death, called for her smelling-bottle and forgot to weep. The sewer extinguishes love: Hero refuses to wash Leander, and Thisbe stops her nose at Pyramus.

title: The Fontis
summary: Valjean wades into the fontis caused by the previous day's rain, unable to turn back, sinking to his calves, waist and armpits while holding Marius above the water like a mother in a painting of the Flood, until with his head alone above the surface his foot strikes the bent but unbroken far edge of the pavement and he climbs out, falls to his knees, and prays.
details: Jean Valjean was facing a fontis. Hugo notes that such quagmires were common in the fluid subsoil of the Champs-Élysées, which in 1836 would hold up the rebuilding of this very sewer under the Faubourg Saint-Honoré for six months amid rain and floods. This one had been made by the downpour of the day before: the sand beneath the pavement had given way, the water had backed up, and the floor had sunk into the ooze to a depth no one could guess. It was a pit of mire in a cavern of night.

Valjean felt the pavement vanish and entered the slime, water on top and mud beneath. Retreat was impossible: Marius was dying and he was exhausted, and where else was there to go? For the first steps it seemed shallow, then the mud reached his calves and the water his knees, then the mud his knees and the water his waist, and he could no longer go back. Mud dense enough to bear one man could not bear two; singly, each might have got out. He went on, holding the dying man, perhaps a corpse, as high as he could. The water reached his armpits and he felt himself sinking, the density that held him up also hindering him; soon only his head was above the water, with his two arms raising Marius, like the mother holding up her child in the old paintings of the Deluge.

He sank further, turned his face backwards to breathe, caught a glimpse of Marius's drooping, livid head above him, made a desperate effort and thrust his foot forward. It struck something solid, a point of support, and high time. He rooted himself on it with a kind of fury, like the first step of a staircase back to life. It was the beginning of the other slope of the pavement, which had bent under the water like a plank without breaking, an inclined plane up which he climbed to the far side of the quagmire. As he came out of the water he struck a stone and fell on his knees, and, reflecting that this was only just, he stayed there some time with his soul absorbed in words addressed to God. Then he rose, shivering, chilled, foul-smelling, bowed under the dying man he dragged after him, dripping with slime and with his soul filled with a strange light.

title: One Sometimes Runs Aground When One Fancies That One Is Disembarking
summary: Drained by the fontis, Valjean staggers on, strikes a wall at a bend and sees far ahead the white light of day; he runs to the outlet on the Seine between the Pont de Jéna and the Pont des Invalides, only to find it closed by a heavy double-locked grating that will not stir, and collapses beside Marius, thinking not of himself but of Cosette.
details: He had left his strength in the fontis if not his life. He had to stop for breath every three or four steps and lean on the wall; once he sat on the banquette to shift Marius and thought he would never rise, but his energy outlived his vigour. Walking on desperately, almost fast, he struck his head against a wall at an elbow of the sewer, looked up, and far away at the end of the vault saw a light, this time not the terrible light of the lantern but good white daylight. Jean Valjean saw the outlet. Like a damned soul glimpsing the way out of Gehenna he ran rather than walked, no longer feeling his fatigue or Marius's weight, towards an arch that narrowed like a funnel, a construction copied from prison wickets.

He reached it and halted. It was the outlet, but he could not get out. The arch was closed by a heavy grating that plainly seldom turned on its rusty hinges, clamped to the stone by a thick lock red with rust like a brick, double-locked, one of the prison locks old Paris loved. Beyond the bars lay the open air, the river, the daylight and a narrow shore, with the Pont de Jéna downstream to the right and the Pont des Invalides upstream to the left, one of the most solitary spots in Paris, opposite the Gros-Caillou, a perfect place to wait for night and escape. Flies came and went through the bars. It was about half past eight in the evening and the day was declining.

He laid Marius on the dry part of the vault and seized the bars with both fists and shook them in a frenzy; nothing moved. He tried each bar in turn, hoping to tear one loose for a lever; not one stirred. No lever, no prying; the obstacle was invincible. He could not retrace his steps through the quagmire he had barely escaped and past a patrol he could not escape twice, and every other outlet was surely barred in the same way; chance had unsealed the grating he came in by, but he had only escaped into a prison. All was over; everything he had done was useless, and exhaustion had ended in failure. Caught with Marius in the great web of death, feeling the spider run along its black strands, he turned his back to the grating and fell to the pavement beside the motionless young man, his head between his knees, at the last drop of anguish. He was thinking neither of himself nor of Marius. He was thinking of Cosette.

title: The Torn Coattail
summary: A barefoot man in a blouse lays a hand on Valjean's shoulder and whispers "Half shares": it is Thénardier, who does not recognise the mud-covered Valjean, takes him for a murderer disposing of a body, offers him a rope for the corpse, takes his thirty francs and secretly tears a strip from Marius's coat, then opens the grating with a key and lets him out onto the shore.
details: In the depths of his prostration a hand touched Valjean's shoulder and a low voice said, "Half shares." He had heard no footsteps and thought he was dreaming, but a man stood before him in a blouse, barefoot, his shoes in his left hand so as to approach unheard. Valjean knew him at once: Thénardier. Steeled to shocks, he recovered himself; nothing could make this night blacker. Thénardier shaded his eyes and screwed them up, trying to recognise the other, and failed: Valjean had his back to the light and was so bemired and bloody that he would have been unrecognisable at noon, while Thénardier stood lit by the cellar-light of the grating. The duel began between Valjean veiled and Thénardier unmasked.

Thénardier asked how he meant to get out, since the lock could not be picked, then explained his terms: "You have killed that man; that's all right. I have the key." He took Valjean for an assassin and a colleague. Give him half of what was in the dead man's pockets and he would open the door; he half drew a huge key from under his blouse to show how a key to liberty is made. Valjean, as Corneille's phrase has it, remained stupid: here was Providence in horrible guise, his good angel springing from the earth in the shape of Thénardier. Thénardier added a rope, explaining to the idiot that he would need a stone too, from the rubbish outside, to sink the stiff in the river, and Valjean took it mechanically. Thénardier chattered on, approving his silence as good practice for the examining magistrate, asking how he had crossed the slough and why he had not tossed the man into it, then answering himself: the workmen would have found the body, but the river is the true grave, Paris the killer, and justice asks no questions. He spoke low, with a finger to his lips and sudden hushes, and Valjean supposed other ruffians lurked nearby with whom he did not care to share.

Asked to show the money, Valjean searched his pockets. He always carried money, but dressing as a National Guardsman the evening before he had forgotten his pocketbook, and he laid on the banquette a louis d'or, two five-franc pieces and five or six large sous. "You knocked him over cheap," said Thénardier, and searched both men's pockets with the greatest familiarity, Valjean letting him so as to keep his back to the light. Handling Marius's coat, Thénardier tore off a strip with a pickpocket's skill and hid it under his blouse, probably thinking it might later identify the murdered man and the murderer; Valjean did not notice. Finding only the thirty francs, Thénardier forgot his motto of half shares and took it all, hesitating only over the sous before pocketing them too, grumbling that people cut throats too cheap altogether.

He helped Valjean get Marius onto his shoulders, crept barefoot to the grating, peered out with a finger on his lips, and turned the key; the gate swung open without a sound. Its oiled hinges showed that it opened more often than anyone supposed, the accomplice of some mysterious band, a receiver of stolen goods. Hugo doubts that Thénardier's intention in letting another man out was purely to rescue an assassin. He opened the gate just wide enough, closed it, double-locked it, and melted back into the dark with the velvet tread of a tiger. Jean Valjean found himself in the open air.

title: Marius Produces on Some One Who Is a Judge of the Matter, the Effect of Being Dead
summary: On the twilight shore Valjean sprinkles river water on Marius's face, turns, and finds Javert behind him with a bludgeon; it was Javert who had been spinning Thénardier, who pushed Valjean out as a decoy. Javert does not recognise him until he gives his name, then, seizing him, hears his one request, to carry Marius home first, reads the address in the pocketbook, calls his waiting coach, and the three drive off towards the Marais.
details: Valjean let Marius slide onto the shore. Behind him lay miasma and darkness; around him the pure evening air, the river flowing at his feet with the sound of a kiss, the nests saying good night in the elms of the Champs-Élysées, the first stars. For a few seconds he was overcome by that caressing serenity and bathed in prayer; then duty returned, and he bent to sprinkle water from his palm on Marius's face. The eyelids did not open, but the half-open mouth still breathed. As he was about to dip his hand again he felt someone behind him and turned. A tall man in a long coat stood a few paces off, arms folded, a leaded bludgeon in his fist. Jean Valjean recognised Javert.

Hugo explains. Thénardier's pursuer had been Javert, who after his unlooked-for release from the barricade had reported to the Prefect in person and gone straight back on duty, which included, as the note found on him had indicated, a surveillance of this stretch of the right bank; there he had seen Thénardier and followed him. The obligingly opened grating was a stroke of cleverness: Thénardier, who sensed that Javert was still there, had flung the sleuthhound a bone, putting an assassin outside in his own place, forcing the police off his scent, earning thirty francs and counting on escaping under cover of the diversion. Valjean had fallen from one danger onto another.

Javert did not recognise the disfigured man and asked who he was. "I." "Who is 'I'?" "Jean Valjean." Javert put his bludgeon between his teeth, clamped both hands on Valjean's shoulders like vices and scrutinised him face to face. Valjean stayed inert like a lion under a lynx's claws and said that Inspector Javert had him in his power, that he had considered himself his prisoner since the morning and had not given his address to escape him; he asked one favour. Javert, in a kind of savage reverie, released him and murmured, as though in a dream, "What are you doing here? And who is this man?", still not addressing him as "thou." Valjean asked only that Javert help him carry the man home before disposing of him as he saw fit. Javert's face contracted as it always did when anyone thought him capable of a concession, but he did not say no. He wet his handkerchief in the river, wiped Marius's bloody brow and said, as if to himself, that this man had been at the barricade and was the one they called Marius; he had played the spy even in his death agony and taken notes. He felt the pulse and pronounced him a dead man. "No. Not yet," said Valjean. Javert's preoccupation must have been profound, for he did not press the question of how the man had been brought from the barricade.

Valjean said the young man lived in the Marais with his grandfather but could not recall the name, and drew out the pocketbook open at Marius's pencilled lines; Javert read them with his night-bird's eyes and muttered the address, Gillenormand, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, No. 6, then shouted for the coachman, whose hackney-coach had been waiting all along. He kept the pocketbook. The carriage came down the watering ramp, Marius was laid on the back seat, Javert sat beside Valjean, and they drove rapidly up the quays towards the Bastille in a glacial silence, the lamplight flashing at intervals on the corpse, the spectre and the statue.

title: Return of the Son Who Was Prodigal of His Life
summary: At night the coach reaches No. 6 Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire; Javert rouses the porter with the news that M. Gillenormand's son has been brought back dead from the barricade, Basque, Nicolette and Aunt Gillenormand are woken while the grandfather sleeps on, Marius is laid on a sofa, and Valjean asks Javert for one more favour, a moment at home, and Javert orders the driver to 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé.
details: A drop of blood fell from Marius's hair at every jolt. Night had fully come when the carriage stopped at No. 6 Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Javert got down first, checked the number, hammered the old knocker with its goat and satyr, and pushed the gate open on a yawning porter with a candle; the whole Marais goes to bed early on days of revolt, hiding its head under the covers like a child who hears the Bugaboo. Valjean and the coachman lifted Marius out, one under the arms and one under the knees, and as they carried him Valjean slipped a hand inside his torn clothes and found the heart beating, a little less feebly than before.

Javert addressed the porter in the tone of government to the servant of a factious house: was there a person called Gillenormand? His son was being brought back. He was dead. Valjean, mud-covered and tattered behind Javert, shook his head at the porter to say it was not so, but the man understood neither. Javert went on: he had gone to the barricade and got himself killed; go and wake his father; there would be a funeral here tomorrow. For Javert, Hugo notes, every incident of the public highway had its drawer: uproar, revolt, carnival, funeral.

The porter woke Basque, Basque woke Nicolette, and Nicolette roused great-aunt Gillenormand; the grandfather they let sleep, thinking he would learn soon enough. Marius was carried to the first floor and laid on an old sofa in M. Gillenormand's antechamber, and while Basque went for a doctor and Nicolette opened the linen presses, Valjean felt Javert touch his shoulder. He understood and went down with Javert's step behind him, the porter watching them go in terrified somnolence. In the carriage Valjean asked Inspector Javert for one more favour: to let him go home for an instant, after which Javert might do with him as he liked. Javert was silent a few moments, chin in his collar, then lowered the front glass and told the driver: Rue de l'Homme Armé, No. 7.

title: Concussion in the Absolute
summary: Valjean, resolved to surrender once he has warned Cosette and settled his affairs, is walked by Javert to his door in the Rue de l'Homme Armé after Javert pays off the coachman; Javert tells him to go up and says he will wait below, but when Valjean leans out of the landing window a moment later, the street is empty: Javert has gone.
details: They did not speak during the drive. Valjean wanted only to finish what he had begun: to warn Cosette, tell her where Marius was, and take what final measures he could. For himself all was over; he had been seized and had not resisted. Another man might have thought of the rope Thénardier had given him and of the bars of his first cell, but since the Bishop there had been in Valjean a profound hesitation before any violence, even against himself, and suicide, a violence against the unknown that may contain the death of the soul, was impossible to him.

The carriage stopped at the mouth of the Rue de l'Homme Armé, too narrow for vehicles. The coachman humbly pointed out to the inspector that his Utrecht velvet was stained with the murdered man's blood and the murderer's mud, that was how he understood it, and asked for an attestation; Javert pushed the certificate book aside, asked the fare for seven and a quarter hours of waiting and driving, eighty francs, paid four napoleons and dismissed him. Valjean supposed Javert meant to walk him to the nearby post of the Blancs-Manteaux or the Archives.

They walked down the deserted street to No. 7. Valjean knocked and the door opened. "It is well," said Javert. "Go upstairs." Then, with a strange expression and as though it cost him an effort: "I will wait for you here." It was unlike Javert's habits, but Valjean, who had made up his mind to give himself up, was not greatly surprised that Javert should show him the haughty confidence of a cat that lets the mouse go to the length of its claws. He called "It is I!" to the porter and climbed the stairs. On the first floor he paused; the landing window was open onto the short street, lit from end to end by the lantern opposite, and he leaned out, for air or mechanically. He was overwhelmed with amazement. There was no longer anyone there. Javert had taken his departure.

title: The Grandfather
summary: The doctor examines Marius, whose wounds are grave but not immediately fatal, while Aunt Gillenormand wrings her hands; M. Gillenormand, woken by the light under his door, appears like a phantom, believes the boy dead, rages that Marius got himself killed to spite him, pours out his love and grief to the doctor, and when Marius slowly opens his eyes cries out his joy and falls fainting.
details: Marius had been carried into the drawing-room and the doctor had come. Aunt Gillenormand went to and fro wringing her hands, saying "Heavens! is it possible?" and that everything would be covered with blood, and at last that it was bound to end this way, stopping short of "I told you so"; when they began undressing Marius she withdrew to tell her beads. The doctor found the pulse beating and no deep wound in the chest, had Marius laid flat on a camp bed with his head low and his chest bare, and took stock: a bullet deadened by the pocketbook had torn round the ribs without entering, the broken collarbone had been badly dislocated by the long underground journey, the arms were slashed by sabre cuts, the face was unmarked but the head was covered with cuts whose depth could not yet be judged, and the swoon and the loss of blood were grave. Basque and Nicolette tore and rolled bandages, wadding stopped the bleeding for want of lint, and a pail of water reddened at once. The doctor shook his head from time to time, a bad sign.

A door opened at the end of the room and a long, pale figure appeared: the grandfather. The revolt had kept M. Gillenormand in a fever for two days; he had gone to bed early, exhausted, and the noise and the rift of light under his door had woken him. He stood on the threshold in a white dressing-gown as straight as a shroud, like a phantom looking into a tomb, and saw on the mattress the young man bleeding, waxen, eyes shut, slashed with crimson wounds under the candles. He trembled from head to foot, his face took the angles of a skull, and he murmured, "Marius!" Basque began to explain that Monsieur had been brought back from the barricade, and the old man cried in a terrible voice, "He is dead! Ah! The rascal!"

A sepulchral transformation straightened him like a young man. He demanded that the doctor tell him whether the boy was dead; the doctor, in the extreme of anxiety, said nothing. Gillenormand broke into terrible laughter: dead, killed on the barricades, out of hatred for him, to spite him, this was how he came home. He threw the window open and harangued the night: the villain knew his room had been kept ready and his childhood portrait hung at the head of his grandfather's bed, that he had only to come back and say "It is I" to be master of the house; and he had said no, the old man is a Royalist, and had gone to get himself killed to avenge a remark about the Duc de Berry. The doctor took his arm, and the old man told him calmly that he was composed, that he had seen Louis XVI die, that it was the newspapers and progress and the rights of man that brought children home like this, and then talked of the child he had raised: his little shovel in the Tuileries, the holes the grandfather filled with his cane so the inspectors would not grumble, the blond head people gathered to admire by the Hercules Farnese, the boy who could not say his Ds and chirped like a bird and was sunlight to him every morning. Children take hold of you and never let go.

Bending over the still, livid Marius he muttered reproaches in the voice of a dying man, heartless lad, clubbist, Septembrist, then, his voice coming as from the far side of an abyss, raged that he would die too, that every girl in Paris would have been glad to make the wretch happy and instead he had gone and got himself shot for the Republic and for General Lamarque's handsome eyes, that there would be two funerals under one carriage gate, that at a hundred years old this blow was what he had hoped for, and that he would not even grieve, did he hear, assassin? At that moment Marius slowly opened his eyes, and his gaze, still dim with lethargic wonder, rested on M. Gillenormand. "Marius! My little Marius! My child! My well-beloved son! You open your eyes, you gaze upon me, you are alive, thanks!" cried the old man, and fell fainting.
